KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) -- With space shuttle Atlantis on its way to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, that leaves one shuttle, Endeavour, at the ready on the other launch pad here. Space shuttle Endeavour, in background, sits poised to launch in case Atlantis, in foreground, meets trouble. And that's where everybody at NASA wants it to stay. "We have high confidence that we're just having that thing over on pad B to make it look nice," said mission flight director Tony Ceccaci. Endeavour is far more than a postcard picture -- it's on standby in case something goes seriously wrong with the Atlantis mission. For example, NASA has estimated there's a 1-in-221 chance the shuttle could be struck and crippled by orbiting space debris. If such an incident were to thrust the seven Atlantis astronauts into danger, Endeavour would blast off within days in a last-ditch attempt to save them. Endeavour Cmdr. Christopher Ferguson believes his crew is up to the task. "I feel as confident about our ability to pull this off, if need be, as I would any other mission," he said. The idea of a standby rescue spacecraft grew out of the 2003 Columbia disaster, in which that shuttle disintegrated over Texas during re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere. But until now, there's been no need. All the previous missions since Columbia have gone to the International Space Station. The crew of a damaged shuttle could take refuge there for months if need be until another shuttle was readied to retrieve them. But Atlantis is going to Hubble, whose orbit isn't anywhere near the space station. If their spacecraft malfunctioned, the seven-member Atlantis crew would have to survive aboard -- probably for days -- until they could be rescued. "In this case it's a much shorter fuse," Ferguson said. "Consumables like food and oxygen would run out quickly. So the reason we've gotten this crew trained and spooled up and ready to go on literally a moment's notice is because they [Atlantis's crew] have no place comfortable to go stay for a long period of time." But the rescue would be no cakewalk. Endeavour would need to pull up underneath Atlantis and hook on to the other shuttle using its robotic arm. Over the course of two days, the seven Atlantis astronauts would spacewalk over to Endeavour by holding on to a tether line strung between the two spaceships. Atlantis mission specialist John Grunsfeld would go first -- and, actually, twice. Grunsfeld would spacewalk to Endeavour, grab an extra EMU (extravehicular mobility unit) spacesuit and take it back to Atlantis. He would then return to Endeavour with one of the Atlantis astronauts not trained in spacewalking. With the Atlantis crew safely aboard, Endeavour would pull away and begin preparing to head home. Atlantis Cmdr. Scott Altman said that knowing Ferguson and the other three members of the Endeavour crew are ready in case of an emergency gives him peace of mind. "Even in the worst-possible imaginable case, we can stay up there and last until somebody comes up and gets us," Altman said. "So it feels like we have all our bases covered." So what would happen to Atlantis? Ferguson said mission leaders would prepare the crippled shuttle for what they call a "disposal burn" -- a safe, remotely controlled landing of Atlantis. "If it comes to it, we certainly don't want a space shuttle coming in over a populated area," he said. "So we want to control the burn so it does end up in the ocean." In all, eleven astronauts would be stuffed into Endeavour. A space shuttle has never carried that many. The four Endeavour crew members would hang out in the flight deck, while the seven Atlantis astronauts would squeeze into the mid-deck area. The journey back to Earth would be uncomfortable. But Ceccaci, the flight director, says that wouldn't matter as long as everyone was safe. "Wrap me in bubble wrap and get me home safely, I wouldn't care," he said. "I wouldn't care how cramped it is."

And that is precisely where everyone at NASA hopes it will remain.

“We have high confidence that we’re just having that thing over on Pad B to make it look nice,” said mission flight director Tony Ceccaci.

Endeavour is far more than a postcard image. It is on standby in case something goes seriously wrong with the Atlantis mission. For example, NASA has estimated there is a 1-in-221 chance that the shuttle could be struck and crippled by orbiting space debris. If such an incident were to put the seven Atlantis astronauts in danger, Endeavour would blast off within days in a last-ditch effort to save them.

Endeavour commander Christopher Ferguson believes his crew is prepared for the task.

“I feel as confident about our ability to pull this off, if need be, as I would any other mission,” he said.

The concept of a standby rescue spacecraft emerged after the 2003 Columbia disaster, in which that shuttle disintegrated over Texas during re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere. Until now, however, such a rescue capability has not been needed. All previous missions since Columbia have gone to the International Space Station. The crew of a damaged shuttle could take refuge there for months, if necessary, while another shuttle was prepared to retrieve them.

But Atlantis is headed to Hubble, whose orbit is nowhere near the space station. If their spacecraft malfunctioned, the seven-member Atlantis crew would have to survive aboard—probably for days—until they could be rescued.

“In this case it’s a much shorter fuse,” Ferguson said. “Consumables like food and oxygen would run out quickly. So the reason we’ve gotten this crew trained and spooled up and ready to go on literally a moment’s notice is because they [Atlantis’s crew] have no place comfortable to go stay for a long period of time.”

But the rescue would be far from simple. Endeavour would have to maneuver beneath Atlantis and connect to the other shuttle using its robotic arm. Over the course of two days, the seven Atlantis astronauts would conduct spacewalks to Endeavour, moving along a tether line strung between the two spacecraft.

Atlantis mission specialist John Grunsfeld would go first—and, in fact, he would make the trip twice. Grunsfeld would spacewalk to Endeavour, retrieve an extra EMU (extravehicular mobility unit) spacesuit, and carry it back to Atlantis. He would then return to Endeavour with one of the Atlantis astronauts not trained in spacewalking.

With the Atlantis crew safely aboard, Endeavour would pull away and begin preparing to return home.

Atlantis commander Scott Altman said that knowing Ferguson and the other three members of the Endeavour crew are ready in the event of an emergency gives him peace of mind.

“Even in the worst-possible imaginable case, we can stay up there and last until somebody comes up and gets us,” Altman said. “So it feels like we have all our bases covered.”

So what would happen to Atlantis? Ferguson said mission leaders would prepare the crippled shuttle for what they call a “disposal burn”—a safe, remotely controlled landing of Atlantis.

“If it comes to it, we certainly don’t want a space shuttle coming in over a populated area,” he said. “So we want to control the burn so it does end up in the ocean.”

In all, eleven astronauts would be packed into Endeavour. A space shuttle has never carried that many people. The four Endeavour crew members would remain on the flight deck, while the seven Atlantis astronauts would squeeze into the mid-deck area.

The journey back to Earth would be uncomfortable. But Ceccaci, the flight director, said that would not matter as long as everyone was safe.

“Wrap me in bubble wrap and get me home safely, I wouldn’t care,” he said. “I wouldn’t care how cramped it is.”

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) — As the shuttle Atlantis travels toward the Hubble Space Telescope for an upgrade mission, another shuttle, Endeavour, is waiting on a separate launch pad at Kennedy Space Center. In photos, Endeavour can be seen in the background, prepared to lift off if Atlantis, visible in the foreground, runs into serious trouble.

NASA, however, hopes Endeavour never has to move.

“We have high confidence that we’re just having that thing over on pad B to make it look nice,” said Tony Ceccaci, the mission’s flight director.

But Endeavour is not merely there for appearances. It is being kept ready as an emergency rescue vehicle if a major problem occurs during Atlantis’ flight. NASA has calculated, for instance, that there is a 1-in-221 possibility that the shuttle could be hit and disabled by debris orbiting Earth. If that kind of accident put Atlantis’ seven astronauts at risk, Endeavour would launch within a few days in a desperate rescue effort.

Christopher Ferguson, Endeavour’s commander, says he trusts his crew’s ability to handle such a mission.

“I feel as confident about our ability to pull this off, if need be, as I would any other mission,” he said.

The plan to have a rescue shuttle prepared came after the 2003 Columbia tragedy, when that shuttle broke apart over Texas while re-entering Earth’s atmosphere. Until this mission, though, NASA had not needed to use such a plan. Every shuttle flight after Columbia had gone to the International Space Station. If one of those shuttles had been damaged, its crew could have stayed aboard the station for months while NASA prepared another shuttle to bring them home.

Atlantis, however, is bound for Hubble, and Hubble’s orbit is nowhere close to the space station. If Atlantis were to fail, its seven astronauts would have to remain inside the damaged shuttle, likely for several days, while waiting for rescue.

“In this case it’s a much shorter fuse,” Ferguson said. “Consumables like food and oxygen would run out quickly. So the reason we’ve gotten this crew trained and spooled up and ready to go on literally a moment’s notice is because they [Atlantis’s crew] have no place comfortable to go stay for a long period of time.”

Carrying out the rescue would be extremely difficult. Endeavour would have to maneuver beneath Atlantis and attach to it with the help of its robotic arm. Then, over a two-day period, the seven astronauts from Atlantis would leave their shuttle during spacewalks and move to Endeavour while gripping a tether stretched between the two spacecraft.

Atlantis mission specialist John Grunsfeld would be the first to make the crossing — and he would do it twice. He would initially spacewalk to Endeavour, pick up an extra EMU, or extravehicular mobility unit spacesuit, and bring it back to Atlantis. After that, he would make the trip to Endeavour again, this time accompanying one of the Atlantis astronauts who had not been trained for spacewalking.

Once all seven Atlantis crew members were safely inside Endeavour, Endeavour would separate and begin getting ready for the return to Earth.

Atlantis commander Scott Altman said it is reassuring to know that Ferguson and the three other Endeavour astronauts are prepared to respond if disaster strikes.

“Even in the worst-possible imaginable case, we can stay up there and last until somebody comes up and gets us,” Altman said. “So it feels like we have all our bases covered.”

As for Atlantis itself, Ferguson said mission managers would set up the damaged shuttle for what they describe as a “disposal burn” — a controlled, remote landing meant to bring Atlantis down safely.

“If it comes to it, we certainly don’t want a space shuttle coming in over a populated area,” he said. “So we want to control the burn so it does end up in the ocean.”

Altogether, Endeavour would carry eleven astronauts, more than any shuttle has ever transported before. The four members of Endeavour’s crew would remain on the flight deck, while the seven rescued Atlantis astronauts would crowd into the mid-deck.

The ride back to Earth would not be comfortable. Still, Ceccaci said comfort would be irrelevant as long as everyone made it home alive.

“Wrap me in bubble wrap and get me home safely, I wouldn’t care,” he said. “I wouldn’t care how cramped it is.”

“This is the kind of preparation we do so the crew can focus on the mission,” a NASA shuttle official said at Kennedy. “We don’t expect to use Endeavour, but if we need it, we need to be ready.”

Atlantis’ astronauts are flying a high-stakes mission to upgrade and repair Hubble, the orbiting observatory that has transformed astronomy since its launch in 1990. The crew’s work includes spacewalks to install new instruments, replace aging components and extend the telescope’s life well into the next decade.

But the Hubble mission is unlike most recent shuttle flights. There is no docking port, no station crew waiting nearby and no place for the astronauts to shelter for weeks if Atlantis suffers serious damage during launch.

That is why Endeavour is positioned at Kennedy Space Center as a lifeboat.

NASA officials say the rescue plan would be activated only if post-launch inspections show Atlantis cannot safely return to Earth. In that scenario, Endeavour would launch with a small crew, rendezvous with Atlantis in orbit and bring the stranded astronauts home.

“Every shuttle mission carries risk,” one NASA manager said. “The difference here is that we’ve had to build the rescue capability into the plan from the start.”

Atlantis’ commander, **Scott Altman**, has said the crew is aware of the unusual backup arrangement but remains focused on Hubble.

“We know the plan is there,” Altman said before launch. “But our job is to go do the mission, take care of the telescope and bring Atlantis home.”

For the astronauts assigned to Endeavour, standing by is a different kind of mission — one built around patience, readiness and the possibility of a rapid call to orbit.

“We train as if we’re going,” an Endeavour astronaut said. “But the best outcome is that Atlantis completes the mission and we stay on the ground.”

The sight of two shuttles on launch pads at the same time has become a striking image at Kennedy Space Center: one orbiter bound for Hubble, the other prepared for an emergency few expect but no one is willing to dismiss.

NASA launch teams say Endeavour’s presence underscores the lessons learned after the 2003 Columbia disaster, when damage to the orbiter’s heat shield led to the loss of seven astronauts during re-entry.

Since then, shuttle crews have performed detailed inspections of their spacecraft in orbit, and NASA has developed repair techniques and rescue plans for worst-case scenarios.

For Hubble, the stakes are scientific as well as human. The telescope’s images have reshaped understanding of the age of the universe, the birth and death of stars, and the existence of galaxies billions of light-years away.

Atlantis’ astronauts are expected to conduct a series of demanding spacewalks, working with tools and components never designed for easy repair in orbit. NASA officials describe the mission as one of the most complex shuttle flights ever attempted.

“This is the last chance to leave Hubble in the best possible shape,” a NASA official said. “It’s a mission with enormous payoff, but we have to be prepared for every contingency.”

If all goes as planned, Atlantis will complete its work, re-enter Earth’s atmosphere and land back in Florida or California. Endeavour would then stand down from rescue duty.

Until then, the second shuttle remains ready — a silent backup on the launch pad while Atlantis reaches for one of NASA’s most treasured spacecraft.

## NASA Readies Rare Shuttle-on-Shuttle Rescue Plan for Atlantis Hubble Mission

**CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. —** In an extraordinary precaution born from the lessons of the Columbia disaster, NASA has prepared a second space shuttle, **Endeavour**, on a neighboring launch pad to serve as a rescue craft for **Atlantis** during the final Hubble Space Telescope servicing mission.

Atlantis is assigned to fly the high-profile Hubble repair mission, known as **STS-125**, carrying seven astronauts to upgrade and extend the life of the orbiting observatory. But unlike most shuttle flights after 2003, Atlantis will not be able to take refuge at the International Space Station if its heat shield is damaged during launch.

That single fact explains the unusual scene at Kennedy Space Center: **two space shuttles standing on two launch pads at the same time**.

### Why Endeavour Is on the Other Pad

Endeavour has been positioned on **Launch Pad 39B** while Atlantis is prepared on **Launch Pad 39A** because NASA must be ready to launch a rescue mission quickly if Atlantis suffers critical damage to its thermal protection system — the fragile tiles and reinforced carbon panels that protect the shuttle during re-entry.

For missions to the International Space Station, a damaged shuttle crew could potentially remain aboard the station while NASA prepared a rescue flight. But the Hubble Space Telescope orbits at a different inclination and altitude than the station. Atlantis cannot simply divert to the ISS; it would not have enough fuel to change orbit and reach it.

As a result, NASA’s backup plan is a dedicated “Launch On Need” rescue mission, designated **STS-400**, using Endeavour.

Keeping Endeavour already stacked, checked out and waiting on a second pad dramatically reduces the time needed to launch a rescue. Without that preparation, NASA would not have enough time to ready another shuttle before Atlantis’ supplies of oxygen, power and other consumables ran dangerously low.

### The Risk NASA Is Guarding Against

The contingency plan is designed for a worst-case scenario: Atlantis reaches orbit, but inspections reveal severe heat-shield damage that would make re-entry too dangerous.

The threat is the same kind of danger that doomed **Columbia** in 2003, when foam debris from the external tank struck the wing during launch. Columbia’s crew was lost when superheated plasma entered the damaged wing during re-entry.

Since then, NASA has required extensive in-orbit inspections after launch. Atlantis’ astronauts would use the shuttle’s robotic arm and inspection boom to examine the wings, nose cap and heat-shield tiles. Engineers on the ground would review high-resolution imagery and sensor data to determine whether Atlantis could safely return.

If the damage were minor, astronauts might attempt repairs in orbit. If NASA concluded the shuttle could not survive re-entry, the rescue plan would be activated.

### How the Rescue Would Work

Under the plan, Endeavour would launch with a small rescue crew rather than a full complement of astronauts. Its mission would be to rendezvous with Atlantis in orbit and bring the stranded crew home.

Because two shuttles cannot dock with each other in the way a shuttle docks with the International Space Station, the rescue would be one of the most complex operations ever attempted in the shuttle program.

The sequence would likely unfold this way:

1. **Atlantis powers down to conserve resources**  
   The Atlantis crew would reduce electrical use and conserve oxygen, water and carbon dioxide removal capability while waiting for Endeavour.

2. **Endeavour launches from the second pad**  
   With Endeavour already prepared at Launch Pad 39B, NASA could launch the rescue mission within a relatively short window, depending on technical readiness, weather and orbital timing.

3. **The two shuttles rendezvous in orbit**  
   Endeavour would carefully approach Atlantis, using standard rendezvous procedures adapted for a shuttle-to-shuttle rescue.

4. **The orbiters station-keep nearby**  
   Since they cannot dock, the two spacecraft would fly in close formation. Robotic arms and carefully planned positioning would help maintain a safe configuration.

5. **Astronauts transfer by spacewalk**  
   Atlantis’ crew would move to Endeavour through a series of EVAs, or spacewalks. The astronauts would wear spacesuits and travel along tethers between the two orbiters. The transfer would be conducted in stages to avoid overcrowding and to maintain safety.

6. **Endeavour returns with both crews**  
   Endeavour would be configured with additional seating and life-support provisions to carry the rescued Atlantis astronauts back to Earth.

7. **Atlantis is abandoned**  
   If Atlantis could not safely re-enter, it would be left uncrewed. NASA would later command it to deorbit in a controlled manner if possible, targeting a remote ocean area.

### A Mission With No Safe Haven

The Hubble servicing flight is considered one of the most important shuttle missions remaining, but also one of the most unforgiving. The telescope is in an orbit that exposes the shuttle to a somewhat higher debris environment than the ISS orbit, and the lack of a space-station refuge makes independent rescue planning essential.

NASA officials have emphasized that the rescue mission is not expected to be needed. It is a precaution — but a highly visible one.

The presence of Endeavour on the neighboring pad is therefore both a symbol of caution and a reflection of NASA’s post-Columbia safety culture. The agency is determined not to send astronauts on a mission without a credible escape plan.

### Why NASA Is Still Sending Atlantis

Despite the risk, NASA considers the Hubble mission worth undertaking. Atlantis’ crew is tasked with installing new instruments, replacing failed components and extending Hubble’s operating life. The work is expected to improve the telescope’s scientific power and keep it functioning for years.

The mission includes multiple spacewalks to perform delicate repairs on a telescope never designed for some of the planned in-orbit servicing tasks.

If successful, the flight will leave Hubble more capable than ever. If something goes wrong with Atlantis, Endeavour will be waiting — a fully prepared lifeboat on the ground, ready to attempt one of the most dramatic rescues in spaceflight history.

**NASA’s High-Wire Hubble Mission: Atlantis to Fly Without Space Station Lifeboat as Endeavour Stands Ready for Rescue**

*Cape Canaveral, Florida* — When space shuttle **Atlantis** blasts off for the Hubble Space Telescope, NASA will be attempting one of the most ambitious and closely watched shuttle missions since the **Columbia disaster** — a flight to repair one of astronomy’s most important instruments, but one that carries a unique risk: there is **no easy place for the astronauts to go if their shuttle is damaged**.

Unlike most post-Columbia shuttle missions, Atlantis will not fly to the **International Space Station**, where a crew could take refuge in an emergency. Hubble orbits at a different altitude and inclination than the station, making a trip from Hubble to the ISS impossible with the shuttle’s available fuel.

That reality has led NASA to prepare a rare backup plan: a second shuttle, **Endeavour**, would be placed on standby as a rescue vehicle.

If Atlantis were damaged during launch or while in orbit and could not safely return through Earth’s atmosphere, Endeavour could be launched on an emergency mission to retrieve the Atlantis crew.

The plan underscores how seriously NASA is treating the flight. The loss of **Columbia in 2003**, when wing damage from foam debris caused the orbiter to break apart during re-entry, reshaped shuttle safety procedures. Since then, NASA has relied on extensive launch imagery, on-orbit inspections, and repair options to reduce the risk of another re-entry catastrophe.

But the Hubble mission presents a tougher challenge.

Because Atlantis cannot reach the space station, NASA’s contingency plan calls for Endeavour to remain ready on a nearby launch pad, prepared for what is known as a **Launch-on-Need** rescue mission. In that scenario, Endeavour would launch with a small crew and rendezvous with Atlantis in orbit.

Once the two shuttles were positioned close together, astronauts would conduct an emergency transfer in space. The crews would use spacesuits and the shuttles’ robotic arms to move astronauts from Atlantis to Endeavour, one by one, in a carefully choreographed operation. Atlantis would then be left behind, while Endeavour returned the combined crew to Earth.

NASA officials have emphasized that such a rescue is considered unlikely. The agency says improvements in inspection and analysis since Columbia have greatly reduced uncertainty about shuttle heat-shield damage. Still, the standby rescue plan is a visible reminder that the Hubble flight carries risks different from other shuttle missions.

The stakes are high. The mission is intended to extend Hubble’s life and improve its scientific power, allowing the telescope to continue producing landmark images and discoveries. Astronauts are expected to perform a series of demanding spacewalks to install new instruments, replace worn components and repair systems never originally designed to be fixed in orbit.

For NASA, the mission is both a scientific opportunity and a test of post-Columbia risk management. Atlantis will fly to a place where no station can provide shelter. Endeavour’s presence on standby is the safety net — one NASA hopes it will never have to use.

# From Kennedy Space Center: Atlantis Launches to Upgrade Hubble as Endeavour Stands Ready for Last-Ditch Rescue

**KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla. —** Space shuttle *Atlantis* thundered away from Florida’s coast Monday on one of NASA’s most ambitious and closely watched shuttle missions: a high-stakes flight to the Hubble Space Telescope intended to extend the observatory’s life and sharpen its view of the universe.

Riding a pillar of flame into a clear sky, *Atlantis* lifted off from Launch Pad 39A with seven astronauts aboard, beginning an 11-day mission to repair and upgrade the orbiting telescope. At a nearby pad, an unusual backup stood in plain view: shuttle *Endeavour*, fueled by contingency planning and ready to launch on short notice if *Atlantis* suffers crippling damage and its crew needs rescue.

The mission is the final planned visit to Hubble, the telescope that has transformed modern astronomy with images of newborn stars, colliding galaxies, distant supernovas and the deep universe. But unlike shuttle trips to the International Space Station, this flight offers no safe haven. Hubble orbits at a different inclination and altitude than the station, meaning the *Atlantis* crew could not reach the outpost if their spacecraft were damaged during launch.

That reality turned an already complex servicing mission into one of the most carefully guarded flights in shuttle history.

“This is a mission we have trained for in extraordinary detail,” said Tony Ceccaci, NASA’s lead flight director for the Hubble servicing flight. “Everybody understands what is at stake — the science, the telescope, and most importantly the crew.”

The *Atlantis* crew is commanded by veteran astronaut Scott Altman, with Gregory C. Johnson as pilot. Mission specialists include John Grunsfeld, Mike Massimino, Andrew Feustel, Michael Good and Megan McArthur. Together, they will attempt five demanding spacewalks to install new instruments, replace batteries and gyroscopes, repair failed electronics and equip Hubble for years of additional observation.

Altman, who previously commanded a Hubble servicing mission, said before launch that the crew was eager to get to work on the telescope.

“Hubble has become part of the way humanity sees itself,” Altman said. “We’re going up there to give it the best possible chance to keep doing that.”

The mission’s headline upgrades include installation of the Wide Field Camera 3, a powerful new instrument designed to observe the universe in ultraviolet, visible and infrared light, and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, which will help scientists study the structure of the universe and the chemical evolution of galaxies. Astronauts also plan to repair the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph and Advanced Camera for Surveys, both of which suffered electronic failures in orbit.

For Grunsfeld, an astronomer-astronaut making another visit to Hubble, the mission is both technical and personal.

“Hubble is a time machine,” Grunsfeld said. “Every time we improve it, we improve our ability to look back across billions of years and ask where we came from.”

NASA managers say the work will be difficult, even by shuttle standards. Some repairs require astronauts to open instrument panels never designed to be serviced in space, remove dozens of tiny fasteners while wearing bulky gloves, and handle delicate electronics in the vacuum of orbit. The spacewalkers have trained for years in underwater mockups and simulators, rehearsing tasks down to individual hand movements.

The stakes are heightened by the fact that Hubble is aging. Launched in 1990, the telescope overcame an early optical flaw to become one of NASA’s most productive scientific instruments. But its systems have been wearing down, and without servicing, agency officials have said Hubble’s ability to conduct cutting-edge science would steadily decline.

“This is not a routine service call,” Ceccaci said. “It is a carefully choreographed expedition to a spacecraft that has already rewritten textbooks.”

While *Atlantis* headed for orbit, *Endeavour* remained poised on Launch Pad 39B as part of a rescue plan NASA calls Launch On Need. The scenario is unlikely, but it is central to the mission’s risk strategy. If inspection after launch finds serious damage to *Atlantis’* heat shield or other critical systems, NASA could prepare *Endeavour* to fly with a four-person crew, rendezvous with *Atlantis*, and bring the astronauts home.

The rescue mission would be commanded by Christopher Ferguson, who has trained for the contingency role while the Hubble crew prepared for the primary mission.

“We hope we never have to launch,” Ferguson said. “But if we are needed, the crew and the vehicle will be ready.”

The presence of two orbiters on two pads is a rare sight and a reminder of the extraordinary precautions surrounding the Hubble flight. After the 2003 *Columbia* disaster, NASA changed how it assessed launch debris, inspected shuttles in orbit and planned for crew rescue. Missions to the space station benefited from the ability to dock and wait for help. Hubble offers no such option.

NASA officials stressed that *Atlantis* underwent intensive preflight analysis and that the launch appeared clean, but the shuttle’s heat shield will be inspected in orbit using cameras and a sensor-tipped boom. Imagery from ground tracking systems, radar and high-resolution photography will also be reviewed by specialists.

Altman said the crew accepted the risks because of the mission’s importance and the preparation behind it.

“We know this mission is different,” he said. “But we also know the teams on the ground have done everything possible to give us the tools, the training and the backup plans we need.”

Once in orbit, *Atlantis* will close in on Hubble over two days. McArthur will use the shuttle’s robotic arm to capture the telescope and berth it in the payload bay, where the astronauts will begin the servicing sequence. Each spacewalk is expected to last more than six hours.

Grunsfeld and Feustel are slated to conduct the first spacewalk, installing the Wide Field Camera 3 and replacing a failed science data handling unit that forced NASA to delay the mission. Subsequent excursions will involve battery replacements, gyroscope work, instrument repairs and the installation of a docking mechanism that will allow a future robotic spacecraft to safely deorbit Hubble at the end of its life.

Scientists around the world are watching closely. If successful, the servicing mission could keep Hubble operating well into the next decade, overlapping with newer observatories and continuing to produce images and data used by researchers across astronomy and astrophysics.

“Hubble has changed what we think is possible,” Grunsfeld said. “It has shown us planets around other stars, galaxies near the dawn of time and the beauty of the universe in a way people everywhere can understand.”

The mission also comes as NASA nears the end of the shuttle program. With the fleet approaching retirement, the Hubble servicing flight carries a sense of finality. For many engineers, flight controllers and astronauts, it represents both the shuttle’s unique capabilities and the risks that defined the program.

Ceccaci said the flight control team is focused on execution, not nostalgia.

“We will have time later to think about history,” he said. “Right now, the job is to fly the mission one step at a time and bring the crew home safely.”

Ferguson and the *Endeavour* rescue crew will remain on alert until NASA is confident *Atlantis* is healthy enough to return on its own. If all goes as planned, *Atlantis* will release Hubble after the upgrades are complete, allowing the telescope to drift free once again above Earth’s atmosphere.

For Altman’s crew, success will mean leaving behind a stronger observatory — one capable of peering deeper into space and further back in time.

“We’re going to visit an old friend,” Altman said. “And when we leave, we hope Hubble will be better than ever.”
